compression.title: The Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library
compression.lede: is the Israel Antiquities Authority's free online library of the Dead Sea Scrolls in images: spectral images of thousands of fragments, among them the oldest known copies of biblical texts, and scans of the 1950s PAM negatives, built with Google, funded by the Leon Levy Foundation and the Arcadia Fund (the site; Friends of the IAA; Wikipedia; the record).

sentences.text: The Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library is the Israel Antiquities Authority's free online library of the Dead Sea Scrolls in images: in its own words it "offers an exceptional encounter with antiquity" and, using "the world's most advanced imaging technology", preserves "thousands of scroll fragments, including the oldest known copies of biblical texts" (deadseascrolls.org.il); the IAA presents it as "a free online digitized virtual library of the Dead Sea Scrolls" (IAA video), and the Revelation First record, which also names it the Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library, files it as a digital library of spectral images of Dead Sea Scroll fragments and 1950s negatives, with introductions to the scrolls (Revelation First record).

Others give it in the same terms: the IAA "has developed" it and its images "can be accessed through various search options on the site" (Orion Center, Hebrew University); a reviewer counts "hundreds of manuscripts and thousands of fragments found in the Judean Desert between 1947 and the early 1960s" (Septuaginta &c., 2014); the Friends of the IAA give "more than 25,000 fragments"; the IAA's channel presents it in a video of four minutes; and the record counts "thousands of scroll fragments" as of 2026-10-30, its first finding the oldest known copies of biblical texts among them (Revelation First record).

What it holds is images: the reader is invited to "examine high-resolution spectral images of manuscript fragments and browse scans of negatives (PAM) from the 1950s" (deadseascrolls.org.il); the record gives its unit as a fragment imaged spectrally with the 1950s PAM scans, its method multispectral imaging and digitized negatives, its evidence manuscript images and catalogue metadata, and names it in its worked question of which manuscripts can be seen directly and which only through an edition, since "an image lets a reader check a reading; an edition reports one" (Revelation First record).

The negatives are older than the library: the Palestine Archaeological Museum acquired most of the Qumran collection, and Najib Albina and the museum's team produced "over 1,750 photographic plates of the scrolls and fragments" (1952–1967), "often considered the best recorded copies of the scrolls" because they recorded the fragments before their further decay in storage (Wikipedia).

The library is not an edition, and holds no New Testament text: the record's negative tags are "NOT an edition: images and introductions" and "NOT a New Testament collection" (Revelation First record); its introductions "follow the journey of the Scrolls from ancient authors, to Bedouin shepherds, and finally to expert scholars and conservators" (deadseascrolls.org.il), through a corpus they give as the religious writings of eleven caves near Qumran and the documents of other sites, most of it "thousands of parchment and papyrus fragments" (the library's introduction).

It is the IAA's, with two funders: the site names "The Leon Levy and Arcadia Funds" among its project pages (deadseascrolls.org.il); the Friends of the IAA give "the generous lead support of the Leon Levy Foundation and additional generous support of the Arcadia Fund"; and the record's operator is "the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA), with the Leon Levy and Arcadia Funds", the library active and maintained by the IAA (Revelation First record).

Google is its partner in the field's account: "the IAA and Google joined forces to develop the most advanced imaging and web technologies" (Friends of the IAA); its first output was "launched together with Google" on 18 December 2012, with digitized images of the 1950s and "about 1,000 images taken with multispectral imaging" (Wikipedia); and the site's footer reads "Powered by:" beside a logo link labelled Google Arts and Culture, under "© 2026 Israel Antiquities Authority" (deadseascrolls.org.il).

The IAA gives the library as its mission, "to make the archaeology and heritage of Israel freely available and accessible to people around the world" (Friends of the IAA), and its general director Shuka Dorfman as preservation for all, so that "the public with a touch of the screen will be able to freely access history in its fullest glamour" (quoted by the Friends of the IAA).

Beside it the field names a distinct collection: the Israel Museum's Scrolls Online, with searchable photographs of the Great Isaiah Scroll, the Community Rule, the War Scroll, the Pesher on Habakkuk and the Temple Scroll (Orion Center), photographed "in partnership with Google" and made available digitally, "albeit not in the public domain" (Wikipedia).

The scrolls it images are mostly Hebrew, "about 15 %" Aramaic and "several in Greek", mainly parchment, some papyrus and one on copper; about 230 are "biblical Scrolls", with copies of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther, and the non-biblical scrolls preserve "a large range of Jewish religious writings from the Second Temple period", apocalyptic texts among them (the library's introduction); the Friends of the IAA count "approximately 1000 different texts" including "the oldest known manuscripts of the five books of the Torah", and the record gives its texts as biblical, apocryphal and sectarian, mostly in Hebrew, with Aramaic and Greek (Revelation First record).

The library dates them: "Scroll dates range from the third century bce (mid–Second Temple period) to the first century of the Common Era, before the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 ce" at Qumran, while scrolls from other sites run from the First Temple period (eighth century BCE) to the eleventh century CE (the library's introduction); the record carries the Qumran range as its second finding and the further sites as earlier and later (Revelation First record); a reviewer gives most of the scrolls the same range (Septuaginta &c.), and Wikipedia cites the library for the consensus range and for Arabic manuscripts of associated sites "dated between the 8th and 10th century CE" (Wikipedia).

The archive reads the Qumran corpus as a sealed Judaism selected against: "981 manuscripts buried in 68 CE" holding "a Judaism with two messiahs, a solar calendar, a priestly hierarchy, a war against Rome", of which "the rabbis who survived did not carry this Judaism forward" (#674), and as a time-locked fracture, "invisible as a coherent sectarian library until the 1947 discovery" (#625).

The record relates the library to the Enoch study, which "dates scrolls from this corpus", and reads it, as the archive's reading, for "the Second Temple literature behind the Apocalypse's imagery, and the corpus on which the Enoch model moved palaeographic dates earlier against radiocarbon anchors" (Revelation First record).

On the text, the library's introduction states that many biblical scrolls resemble the Masoretic Text though "over a thousand years older than previously identified biblical manuscripts", that "additions and deletions in certain texts imply that the writers felt free to modify texts they were copying", that the refuge-cave scrolls suggest the text "was stabilized by the second-century ce", and that the scrolls' communities "did not have a unified conception of an authoritative collection of scriptural works" (the library's introduction).

The archive reads the Masoretic Bible as "a medieval stabilization" of "one textual stream among several that coexisted at Qumran" (#978), the Masoretes having "fixed one textual stream and closed the others" where "Qumran held two editions of Jeremiah, a Samuel that agreed with the Greek, an Isaiah that varied line by line" (#674), and seats the biblical scrolls as "witnesses against the Leningrad seat (01/09), not duplicates of it" (#1531).

Which communities the scrolls represent is disputed: the introduction states "disagreement" about "which communities are represented and how those communities may have interacted with one another", and that the attribution of all the Qumran scrolls to the Essenes, once the consensus, "has been challenged and modified" (the library's introduction); the record finds the library's limits "none stated in the saved pages" (Revelation First record); and the archive reads the classification itself, holding that the filing of Qumran under "sectarianism" "is disposal continued by other means" (#674).

The archive reads the Qumran scribes as composers: "The sectarian scribe is not a mere copyist. The scribe is a co-speaker with the logos" (#978); of the Slavonic Josephus's Essene passages, "all of it aligns with practices documented in the Qumran scrolls, particularly the Community Rule (1QS) and the Damascus Document (CD)" (#626); in the scrolls "the Yahad practiced strict initiation with symbolic role reassignment" and the Teacher of Righteousness "functions as a Logos-like figure" (#1101); and the groups the scrolls preserve "practiced a form of apocalyptic that was not merely predictive but operative", the War Scroll "a battle plan" (#861).

On the Revelation First thesis, a hypothesis the archive states with its falsifiers, the scrolls' literature stands behind the Apocalypse: Revelation "compresses the Hebrew prophetic tradition, Second Temple apocalyptic, imperial resistance, liturgical form, and cosmic architecture into a single seed-text", its commentary annotating connections "to Second Temple literature (1 Enoch, 4 Ezra)" (#832); the Revelator "constructs a vision cosmology aligned with Qumran/Enoch/Daniel", compressing the architecture of Second Temple Judaism into "a portable, sealed, self-decompressing form" (#1101), in "a scribal workshop continuous with Qumran practice, predating the gospels" on the Josephus Thesis reading (#978); and the archive maps the received literature that reads the War Scroll, the pesharim and "apocalyptic sectarianism" as "structural parallels to Revelation" (#644).

The thesis sets its own limit on this literature: its transforms must be shown "not reducible to generic literary influence or shared Second Temple background (the common-substrate confound)", and if they "operate equally well from Ezekiel/Daniel to both Revelation and Paul independently", they establish "only shared ancestry" (#832).

The archive reads the Qumran library as "the canonical antecedent of the present framework's deposit-and-provenance discipline", its choosing, copying and sealing "for transmission across substrate-change" anticipating the archive's deposits, and holds its own deposit methodology "written-from-within the Qumran preservation tradition" (#152).

Access is by image and search: a reviewer describes "the multi-criteria archive search page, where users can sort by archaeological site, language, scroll content", material, historic period and manuscript type, with "just over 130" Greek items (Septuaginta &c.); the library is linked to the Orion Bibliography, and Scripta Qumranica Electronica combines "the digital images of all known Qumran fragments" at the library with the Qumran dictionary's data (Orion Center); the record gives images and negatives online, its licence "its Terms & Conditions (not read)", the fragment records unchecked (Revelation First record).

As a source of text it was closed to the archive's machines: "the Leon Levy Digital Library returns 403", and the Qumran corpus, "transcribed decades ago, publicly funded", is "not openly machine-readable", declared the largest gap in the openly licensed record "with a date against it" (#1522, 2026-08-21); the archive seated the scrolls' text instead from the Abegg–Bowley–Cook transcriptions, "1,001 scrolls, 1.43M signs", the corpus that "spent forty years behind a publication monopoly, liberated in 1991 by Abegg's reconstruction from the concordance" (#1531).

The IAA keeps the scrolls in a climate-controlled storeroom and laboratory in the Rockefeller Museum, its project since its creation in 1990, where "each fragment is photographed and mapped" (Friends of the IAA).

In the Revelation First field, organized by the question "What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?" and its correction "Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early", the library stands at papyrology and textual discovery and at New Testament scholarship; it answers what a fragment looks like in spectral images and the date range it gives the scrolls, and does not answer the composition of the New Testament writings or a particular fragment's date (Revelation First record).
Wikipedia has no article on the library under its name and lists it among the scrolls' online sources (Wikipedia).

At its own name on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-31, a new address whose record was built the day before and is cited by no card, the composition gave who made the library, how it images the scrolls, what it holds and how to search it, "from the library's site and those of its friends", the IAA as maker, the spectral images and the PAM negatives being the record's (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31; Revelation First record).

The registry records the composition naming Google as partner, "a partner the records do not state", and omitting "the funds whose name the library bears" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31); in the field the partner and the funders are one sentence, the Friends of the IAA's, of which the composition kept the second half, and Wikipedia states the launch with Google (Friends of the IAA; Wikipedia).

The registry records the dates absent, the composition dating "the discovery (1947 to the early 1960s)" and giving "the scrolls no date", and reads "a library of dated objects" composed "as a database without its dates" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31); the range stands in the library's introduction and on the second card (the library's introduction; Septuaginta &c.).

The registry finds "'12 different wavelengths' and the list of search filters" not in the saved pages (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31); the search filters and the discovery years are on the second and sixth cards, and no field source gives the wavelengths (Septuaginta &c.; IAA video).
